Shoulder and Posterior Arm

Daniel Hannah, PhD, ATC · Based on the 57 lecture slides and 9 pages of 2026 accompanying notes

← Week 14 HubCondensed Factoid01 · Shoulder complex & osteology02 · Sternoclavicular & acromioclavicular joints03 · Glenohumeral joint: mobility & stability04 · Shoulder muscles & their actions05 · Rotator cuff mechanics & scapulohumeral rhythm06 · Posterior arm & triceps07 · Nerve pathways, sensory territories & injury08 · Arterial supply & anastomoses09 · Anatomical spaces: clinical map10 · Additional lecture-note clinical correlations
Core idea: Shoulder function requires simultaneous mobility and stability. The SC/AC joints position the scapula; the labrum/capsule and rotator cuff stabilize the highly mobile glenohumeral joint; the axillary and radial neurovascular routes explain classic injury patterns.

01 · Shoulder complex & osteology

The shoulder is designed to maximize mobility while preserving stability. It anchors the highly mobile upper limb to the axial skeleton and transmits load back toward the trunk. The bony chain is the clavicle (sternoclavicular and acromioclavicular articulations), scapula (glenoid), and humerus.

Clavicle

S-shaped, subcutaneous, palpable throughout. Fractures often follow a direct shoulder fall or fall on an outstretched hand. The lecture emphasizes the middle third / junction of middle and lateral thirds. Sternocleidomastoid elevates the medial fragment, while the unsupported shoulder/lateral fragment drops.

Scapular landmarks

Acromion, coracoid, suprascapular notch, glenoid fossa, spine, subscapular / supraspinous / infraspinous fossae, supraglenoid (long-head biceps) and infraglenoid (long-head triceps) tubercles; the spinoglenoid notch is also shown.

Humeral landmarks

Greater tubercle (SIT insertions), lesser tubercle (subscapularis), intertubercular groove (long-head biceps tendon), anatomical/surgical necks, deltoid tuberosity, posterior radial groove, olecranon fossa. The ulna contributes the olecranon, insertion for triceps.

Fracture mapping: surgical neck → axillary nerve + posterior circumflex humeral artery; humeral shaft/radial groove → radial nerve + profunda (deep) brachii artery. The lecture shows both fractures on radiographs (slides 56–57).

02 · Sternoclavicular & acromioclavicular joints

SC jointAC joint
Joint typeSaddle synovial (functions multiaxially); the sole bony articulation linking upper limb to axial skeletonPlane synovial joint between lateral clavicle and acromion
SupportsInterclavicular resists inferior translation; sternoclavicular ligaments resist anterior/posterior translation; costoclavicular resists superior translationAC ligament supports joint; coracoclavicular ligament is principal stabilizer, comprising conoid + trapezoid
DiscFibrocartilage disc partitions joint into two cavities; shock absorption and congruenceDisc may be variable / incomplete; slide notes a complete disc in ~10% of adults
ClinicalRare displacement; posterior dislocation endangers deep structures (clinical inference)Shoulder separation: AC ligament injury; greater injury tears coracoclavicular support and creates obvious step-off

When AC stabilizers fail, gravity drops the scapula/upper limb relative to the clavicle, making the clavicle appear elevated. Distinguish shoulder separation (AC) from shoulder dislocation (glenohumeral).

03 · Glenohumeral joint: mobility & stability

The glenohumeral joint is a highly mobile ball-and-socket articulation between the humeral head and shallow glenoid. The professor notes that only ~30% of the humeral head contacts the glenoid in any one position: excellent motion, inherently limited osseous stability.

  • Glenoid labrum: fibrocartilaginous ring that deepens the glenoid socket by approximately 50%; superior labrum is anatomically related to the long-head biceps origin.
  • Fibrous capsule: lax and capacious, attached to glenoid rim and anatomic neck (slightly more distal inferiorly), enabling movement and translation.
  • Static supports: coracohumeral ligament, superior/middle/inferior glenohumeral ligaments, and the superior coracoacromial arch.
  • Dynamic supports: long-head biceps tendon and SITS rotator cuff; active compression centers the humeral head.
  • Subacromial space: ~1 cm in the slides; contains supraspinatus tendon region, subacromial/subdeltoid bursa, long-head biceps tendon region, and superior capsule; associated with friction reduction and impingement.
GH dislocation: lecture states ~90% anterior. Assess and document axillary nerve and arterial/neurovascular status before and after reduction. Anterior-inferior weakness permits displacement; the coracoacromial arch resists superior displacement.

The scapulothoracic interface is not a true synovial articulation. Scapular translation/rotation depends on coordinated SC/AC movement.

04 · Shoulder muscles & their actions

MuscleOrigin → insertionMajor actionNerve
DeltoidLateral third clavicle, acromion, spine scapula → deltoid tuberosityAnterior: flex / medial rotate; middle: abduct; posterior: extend / lateral rotateAxillary (C5–6)
Teres majorInferior angle scapula → medial lip intertubercular grooveAdduct / medial rotate humerusLower subscapular (C5–6)
SupraspinatusSupraspinous fossa → superior facet greater tubercleInitiate abduction, stabilizationSuprascapular (C5–6)
InfraspinatusInfraspinous fossa → middle facet greater tubercleLateral rotation, stabilizationSuprascapular (C5–6)
Teres minorMiddle lateral scapular border → inferior facet greater tubercleLateral rotation, stabilizationAxillary (C5–6)
SubscapularisSubscapular fossa → lesser tubercleMedial rotation / adduction, stabilizationUpper & lower subscapular (C5–6)
SITS = supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis. SIT attach to greater tubercle, S attaches to lesser tubercle. Teres major is not a cuff muscle.

05 · Rotator cuff mechanics & scapulohumeral rhythm

The rotator cuff does more than rotate the arm: it generates a compressive stabilizing force that holds the humeral head against the glenoid, keeps it centered/inferior enough during elevation, and clears the greater tubercle beneath the acromion. The deltoid and cuff operate as a force couple.

Scapulohumeral rhythm: a useful approximation is 2:1 GH motion : scapulothoracic upward rotation. For 180° elevation, roughly 120° is glenohumeral and 60° scapular rotation (ratio varies and the accompanying notes describe an early-setting phase). Trapezius and serratus anterior position the scapula.

Most common rotator cuff tear: supraspinatus, associated with repetitive overhead activity. Difficulty initiating abduction and impaired GH stability. Slides 40–41 contrast normal vs torn supraspinatus on coronal MRI and illustrate disruption of the deltoid–cuff force couple.

06 · Posterior arm & triceps

Triceps headProximal attachment
LongInfraglenoid tubercle of scapula
LateralPosterior humerus superior to radial groove
MedialPosterior humerus inferior to radial groove

All three heads attach distally to the olecranon of ulna and are innervated by the radial nerve. Main action: elbow extension; long head also contributes to shoulder extension/adduction and resistance to dislocation. The accompanying notes also mention anconeus: lateral epicondyle → lateral olecranon, radial nerve, assists/stabilizes elbow extension.

The profunda (deep) brachii artery leaves brachial artery and accompanies the radial nerve in the humeral radial groove. This is the basis of the classic midshaft fracture risk.

07 · Nerve pathways, sensory territories & injury

NerveKey targets & findings
Suprascapular (from superior trunk)Supraspinatus + infraspinatus; passes under superior transverse scapular ligament at suprascapular notch
Axillary (posterior cord)Deltoid + teres minor; cutaneous lateral shoulder/“regimental badge”; surgical-neck fracture/anterior GH dislocation → weak abduction, flattened shoulder, sensory loss
Upper / lower subscapular (posterior cord)Subscapularis (both); teres major (lower)
Thoracodorsal (posterior cord)Latissimus dorsi
Radial (posterior cord)Triceps, posterior arm and forearm extensors; posterior arm cutaneous and posterolateral hand regions
“Army over, Navy under” the superior transverse scapular ligament: suprascapular artery above, suprascapular nerve below.

08 · Arterial supply & anastomoses

Subclavian-side contributions: suprascapular artery (from thyrocervical trunk or subclavian) and dorsal scapular artery. Axillary-side contributions: thoracoacromial artery (clavicular, acromial, deltoid, pectoral branches), subscapular artery → circumflex scapular and thoracodorsal, plus anterior and posterior circumflex humeral arteries.

Scapular anastomosis: dorsal scapular ↔ suprascapular ↔ circumflex scapular permits collateral flow around a proximal axillary blockage; collateral compensation may be more effective for slow than sudden occlusion. Acromial anastomosis includes posterior circumflex humeral and acromial thoracoacromial contributions, as depicted in the lecture.

In the posterior arm, brachial artery gives profunda brachii alongside radial nerve; its radial collateral continuation joins a radial recurrent branch distal to the elbow.

The lecture closes with two radiographic applications: shaft fracture → radial nerve / deep brachial artery and surgical neck fracture → axillary nerve / posterior circumflex humeral artery.

10 · Additional lecture-note clinical correlations

SC dislocation: rare because of very strong ligamentous stabilization; the lecture notes distinguish incomplete injury from combined sternoclavicular/costoclavicular disruption.

AC separation: isolated AC injury produces a milder subluxation; AC + coracoclavicular injury produces more severe separation with superiorly prominent clavicle.

Hilton’s law: nerves supplying muscles moving a joint generally give articular branches to that joint and cutaneous supply near the joint. The supplied notes list suprascapular, axillary, pectoral, musculocutaneous, subscapular, thoracodorsal and radial nerves in the shoulder pain/proprioception discussion.

Adhesive capsulitis: thickening and contracture/scarring of GH capsule causes painful stiffness and restricted abduction, with diabetes and prolonged immobilization noted as risks.

Cross-sectional image learning objective: focus on recognizing bones, tendons, joint space, neurovascular relationships and the MRI supraspinatus comparison. The slides contain explicit X-rays and MRI; they do not present a dedicated CT interpretation series.

Active-recall checkpoints

Why is the glenohumeral joint intrinsically unstable?

Shallow glenoid; the lecture notes ~30% humeral-head contact at any moment, demanding labral, capsular and cuff support.

What is the primary coracoclavicular ligament contribution at the AC joint?

Primary stabilizer; composed of conoid and trapezoid bands.

What separates shoulder separation from dislocation?

Separation = AC; dislocation = GH.

Which four muscles comprise SITS?

Supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis.

What is the 2:1 scapulohumeral rhythm approximation?

For every 2 degrees GH elevation, 1 degree scapular upward rotation: about 120° GH + 60° scapular for full 180°.

Which structures travel through the quadrangular space?

Axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery.

Which structures travel through the triangular interval?

Radial nerve and profunda brachii artery.

What neurovascular structures are at risk with surgical-neck vs shaft fractures?

Surgical neck: axillary nerve / posterior circumflex humeral artery. Shaft: radial nerve / deep brachial artery.

What runs above vs below the superior transverse scapular ligament?

Suprascapular artery above, suprascapular nerve below.

Why can scapular collaterals protect blood flow?

Connections between dorsal scapular, suprascapular and circumflex scapular arteries link subclavian and axillary regions.
